question: The European Commission has just introduced the ‘environmental omnibus’, which rolls back environmental legislation on the grounds of increasing businesses’ competitiveness. The proposal would be a very serious environmental setback, as well as an attack on the Aarhus Convention’s principles regarding environmental protection and the right to good administration.

It would also exacerbate the already existing lack of transparency, as is being seen with strategic projects being awarded to the benefit of various industrial and mining lobbies, and which would seriously endanger people’s and ecosystems’ health.

Given that the European Ombudsman has agreed to examine a complaint by civil society about the lack of transparency in access to documents on the environmental impacts of projects designated as strategic projects under the Critical Raw Materials Act: 1.

How does the Commission intend to ensure both compliance with the Aarhus Convention and the active participation of civil society and the affected communities in public consultations, at the same time as simplifying procedures?

How does the Commission intend to guarantee both the right to good administration and that the environmental impact of environmentally sensitive projects is correctly assessed, so as to prevent extractivist practices in Europe?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.3.2026) The Commission would point out that the Omnibus package, currently under examination of both co-legislators, does not intend to lower environmental standards.

Its aim is to simplify environmental legislation in the areas of industrial emissions, circular economy, environmental assessments and geospatial data without undermining the existing environmental standards and policy objectives.

The proposed changes are expected to contribute to reducing the administrative burden for businesses, while keeping the EU's ambitious objectives to protect the environment and human health. The Commission believes that the Aarhus Convention remains a milestone for environmental good governance in the Union and beyond.

The proposal, therefore, preserves the Aarhus principles, as Article 13 of the proposal for a Regulation on speeding-up environmental assessments1 underlines. In line with these principles, the Critical Raw Materials Act2 also preserves the applicability of the Aarhus Convention, as confirmed by its Article 14.
1 COM(2025) 984 final. 2 Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 establishing a

framework for ensuring a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials and amending Regulations (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1724 and (EU) 2019/1020, OJ L, 2024/1252, 3.5.2024.
